bio.en: Matt Abrahams is a Stanford Graduate School of Business lecturer on communication and the host of the Think Fast, Talk Smart podcast, and author of a popular book on speaking confidently.
bio.zh: 马特·亚伯拉罕斯（Matt Abrahams）是斯坦福商学院的沟通课程讲师、Think Fast, Talk Smart 播客的主持人，也是一本关于自信演讲的畅销书作者。

summary.en: Matt teaches that you must "prepare to be spontaneous" through practice, just like athletes or jazz musicians. He recommends visualization to calm anxiety and striving for connection over perfection by "daring to be dull." The episode is a practical toolkit for communicating clearly and confidently in the moment.
summary.zh: 马特指出，你必须像运动员或爵士乐手那样，通过练习来"为即兴做准备"。他推荐用可视化来缓解焦虑，并通过"敢于平淡"来追求连接而非完美。本期是一套关于在当下清晰、自信沟通的实用工具箱。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Visualization is a really useful technique and you see yourself not just in the moment of speaking, but getting up to the stage, seeing it being well received, thinking about how you step off the stage. We see athletes do this kind of thing all the time, and there's good research to say that this desensitizes people.
turns.zh: 视觉化是一种非常有效的技巧。你要想象自己不仅是在演讲的当下，还要构想登上舞台、获得热烈反响的场景，甚至设想自己走下舞台的时刻。我们经常看到运动员这样做，相关研究表明，这种做法能帮助人们增强抗压能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Most of the public speaking we do is on the spot. It's not often you give a prepared talk.
turns.zh: 大多数公开演讲都是即兴发挥的，很少有机会提前准备讲稿。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: You actually have to prepare to be spontaneous. And that's counterintuitive, but when you think about it in athletics or jazz music, it's like of course you would prepare and practice.
turns.zh: 实际上，你必须先做好准备，才能做到自然流畅。这听起来有些矛盾，但若以体育运动或爵士乐为例，就会发现人们显然会通过充分准备和刻意练习来提升表现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any other techniques that you love that you find people find really helpful in calming their anxiety?
turns.zh: 还有哪些技巧能帮助人们缓解焦虑感？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Strive for connection over perfection by daring to be dull. Just answer the question. Just give the feedback. Just be engaged in the small talk. By doing that, you dial down the volume of self-evaluation, freeing up resources that can be used to really help you succeed.
turns.zh: 敢于平凡，努力建立联系而非追求完美。只需回答问题、提供反馈、参与闲聊。这样做能降低自我评判的负担，将精力投入到真正助力成功的行动中。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Absolutely, I look forward to that and those are topics I'm very excited to talk about, have done a lot of research in and look forward to sharing more.
turns.zh: 太好了。我也很期待讨论这些主题。我对此做了大量研究，也写了一本书，正期待能与你分享更多心得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I suspected as much. Okay, so let's talk about anxiety. You have a bunch of really novel techniques in your book and your podcast for calming your body down, calming your mind down when you're planning to give a talk, when you're actually about to give a talk, when you're giving a talk. And a lot of these I haven't actually seen anywhere else and I've used a few of them and they are really great. So what I was thinking we'd do is let me go through the ones that I found most useful and interesting and just share your advice on those and then see if there's any I missed and then maybe add those at the end. How's that?
turns.zh: 我也这么想。好的，那我们先聊聊焦虑管理。你在书和播客里提到了很多新奇的技巧，能帮助演讲者在准备演讲前、演讲时、演讲后平复身心。我在其他地方没见过这些方法，自己也用过几个，效果确实不错。接下来我想，我们可以先讲讲我觉得最实用、最有趣的技巧，再听听你的建议，最后看看有没有遗漏的可以补充。这样如何？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: That sounds great. That sounds great. I love that you've applied some of these techniques and found value from them.
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。我很欣赏你实际应用了这些技巧，并从中获得了价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll talk about this, I'll talk about this. Okay, first of all, just to catch on this, you're not a fan of the picture people in your audience naked approach, correct?
turns.zh: 我会详细讲讲这个问题。首先，确认一下，你不赞成让观众想象自己裸体的方法，对吧？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: The Brady Bunch advice is not good advice. I don't know about you and I don't know anybody who could imagine seeing a bunch of people in their underwear and feel more comfortable with that. And I think if you do, there are other issues you need to be dealing with than beyond speaking anxiety.
turns.zh: 《布雷迪家庭》的建议可不靠谱。我不知道你怎么想的，但我认识的人没人能想象看到一群人穿着内衣会觉得更自在。如果你真能想象到这种场景，那你需要处理的恐怕不只是演讲焦虑了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it feels like highly inappropriate now, just that idea, trying to picture everyone-
turns.zh: 是啊，现在看来这种想法太不合适了。光是想象别人半裸的画面——

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: No, but underlying that if you'll give me a moment, there is some value. This notion of visualization as a tool of desensitization actually can be very helpful, but you're not visualizing the audience half naked. What you're doing is you're visualizing yourself in that space. You're visualizing the audience responding to you and what you're saying. So just like a pilot might do a flight simulator, having a visualization can actually really help you feel more comfortable and confident. It literally puts you in the room even though you're not there. And there's some tools and I'm fascinated by these tools that are virtual reality tools that can also serve to desensitize you. So this notion of seeing your audience in advance of actually speaking can actually impact your level of comfort. It's let's keep everybody clothed and let's keep them all focused on your topic.
turns.zh: 不，但深层逻辑是，如果你能稍等片刻，这里面还是有价值的。把可视化作为脱敏工具的概念确实很有用，但你想象的不是观众半裸的样子，而是自己在那个场景中的样子，想象观众对你的反应和你的发言。所以就像飞行员会进行飞行模拟一样，可视化能帮助你增强自信和舒适感。它能让你身临其境，即便你实际上并不在现场。还有一些工具，比如虚拟现实工具，也能帮助你脱敏。所以在实际演讲前想象观众的样子，确实能影响你的舒适度。还是让大家都穿着整齐，专注于你的演讲内容吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's actually talk about this one while we're on it because I think this is a really powerful technique. An idea just to kind of summarize, you picture ahead of time, what it's going to look like and feel like. You talking, looking at the audience. You talk about that and just how to go about using that technique.
turns.zh: 好的，我们来具体聊聊这个技巧吧，因为我觉得它真的很有效。简单来说，你要提前想象演讲时的场景和感觉——你站在台上演讲，看着听众，描述整个过程，以及如何运用这个技巧。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And this is some of the oldest research on public speaking anxiety. It was research done in the '80s from the University of Oregon. So visualization, what it does is it allows you to see the event in a way that you have much more control over it so you can think about it. So a good visualization involves some deep breathing to calm yourself. Either you close your eyes or you just look at a picture. Maybe you can get a picture of the environment you're speaking in. I often recommend speakers see the room even if they're not physically present, but get a picture online or some way envision yourself in the room, envision yourself in the room with the people you'll be speaking to. Often we know the individuals or some of them. We can also go online and figure out who they are. (00:08:39): So visualization is a really useful technique and you see yourself not just in the moment of speaking but getting up to the stage, delivering the presentation, seeing it being well received, thinking about how you step off the stage. And by taking yourself through that you in essence are a dress rehearsal even though you're not physically in the room. And there's good research to say that this desensitizes people. We see athletes do this kind of thing all the time where they'll do visualization to help them and it really does work. And like I said, there are virtual tools now that can help you do this where you can actually program it to have a certain size audience. You can even program some of these to have a responsive audience or a distracted audience. All of this in service of just preparing you for what you're really going to see. (00:09:25): And the bottom line is this, what you're doing for yourself is making sure it's not new and novel. It's something been there, done that, even though if it was virtual or visualized in your mind, to help you feel better about the circumstance. It gives you a sense of agency.
turns.zh: 没错。这是关于演讲焦虑最早的研究成果之一，来自80年代俄勒冈大学的研究。视觉化训练能让你更有效地掌控演讲场景，所以需要深呼吸放松。可以闭上眼睛想象，或直接看相关图片。比如想象演讲环境，设想自己与听众的互动。（00:08:39）：这种想象练习非常实用，它能让你预演整个演讲过程——从登台到演讲结束，再到下台。通过这种模拟演练，即便你实际不在现场，也能提前适应环境。研究表明，这种方法能帮助人们消除紧张情绪。我们经常看到运动员通过视觉化训练提升表现，确实有效。现在还有虚拟工具能模拟不同观众反应，比如热情回应或冷漠反应，帮助你提前适应真实场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've done this myself actually. I gave a TEDx talk once and it was probably the scariest talk I've ever given and I spent a lot of time doing this and it doesn't actually have to take that much time. It could be like a five-minute thing where you sit down, calm yourself, and then just picture the stuff. And ideally you do it a couple times, I imagine.
turns.zh: 我自己也试过一次。当时我在TEDx做演讲，那是我最紧张的一次。花了大量时间准备视觉化练习，实际上只需要五分钟：坐下来，放松心情，然后在脑海中构想整个场景。最好多练习几次。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: That's right. Good for you. And congratulations on giving a TEDx talk. That is a high-stakes talk.
turns.zh: 没错，很棒。恭喜你完成TEDx演讲，这可是高难度任务。

turns.en: Don't say they're uncool. I'm doing one in two weeks.
turns.zh: 别说它过时了。我两周后也要做一场TEDx演讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're so cool. That is, they are cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。确实很酷。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're incredible. I'm impressed.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很佩服。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: I've done a number of them and I've coached many people and I think that there's a lot of value that they can provide people.
turns.zh: 我做过不少这类活动，也指导过很多人，觉得它们能为人们带来很大价值。

turns.en: There is. There is. I think they've just become slightly less cool because now there's a lot of them, but they're still incredibly cool, I'm very proud.

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Okay, thank you.
turns.zh: 好的，谢谢。

turns.en: So on the visualization piece, I think we have a lot of techniques, but just on this one, part of it is continue to calm yourself as you're doing it. I think that's really important because you want to help your body not connect to the stress that you're feeling like you're going to experience.
turns.zh: 关于可视化部分，我认为我们有很多技巧，但就这一部分而言，关键在于在操作过程中保持冷静。我觉得这很重要，因为你要帮助自己的身体不要去感知即将经历的压力。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: That's correct. Any distance you can give yourself from the anxiety that you're feeling is helpful and there are lots of techniques that help give you a little bit of distance and visualization is one of those.
turns.zh: 没错。你能给自己的焦虑留出一点距离，这很管用，而可视化就是其中一种方法。

turns.en: One of my favorite techniques that it might be in this bucket, it might be on the spot advice bucket, but I think it works great here is what you call dare to be dull. Can you talk about that because I love that?
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的技巧之一，可能属于即兴演讲范畴，但我觉得在这里也很适用，那就是所谓的“敢于平庸”。你能讲讲这个吗？因为我很喜欢这个理念。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah. I really leaned into this with the spontaneous speaking work that I've been doing as of late, but it applies to anybody speaking. This is a notion that comes from the world of improvisation and when people hear improv, they often think of standup comedy, having to be funny. And that's not what improv is all about. Improv is all about being present, being collaborative, being open, and it's a wonderful tool just to help you get present oriented. Think of it as like meditation in action, but also it teaches lots of valuable skills for communication. (00:11:42): When we communicate, especially spontaneously, we want to do it really well. We want to answer the question with the best answer, we want to give the right feedback, we want to be the most interesting in small talk and that puts a lot of pressure on ourselves. And you can think of it this way, it's really taxing our cognitive bandwidth. (00:12:04): Your brain in many ways is like a CPU, a computer. It's not a perfect analogy, but it works. And if I am constantly judging and evaluating everything I am saying against some standard of perfection, whatever that is, it means I have a limited amount of bandwidth to focus on what I'm actually saying and connecting to my audience. If you have a laptop or a phone that has lots of windows and apps open, each one of those is performing less well because of the other ones being open. So I often say strive for connection over perfection by daring to be dull. Just get the task done, just answer the question, just give the feedback, just be engaged in the small talk. And by doing that you dial down the volume of self-evaluation, freeing up resources that can be used to really help you succeed. So dare to be dull is all about giving yourself permission to just be present and do what's needed. And when you do that you find that you actually do quite a good job at it.
turns.zh: 是的。最近我在做即兴演讲时深入研究了这个技巧，但它适用于任何演讲场合。这个理念源自即兴表演领域。人们一提到即兴表演，往往会想到单口喜剧，觉得必须搞笑。但这并非即兴表演的核心。即兴表演强调当下感、合作精神和开放心态，它是帮助你专注当下的绝佳工具。可以把它视为行动中的冥想，同时还能培养宝贵的沟通技能。（00:11:42）：在交流时，尤其是即兴交流时，我们总想表现得完美。我们想用最佳答案回应问题，给出恰当反馈，在闲聊中成为最有趣的人，这会给自己带来巨大压力。换个角度看，这其实是在消耗我们的认知带宽。（00:12:04）：大脑在很多方面就像电脑的中央处理器。虽然比喻不完美，但这个比喻能说明问题。如果我总是在说每一句话时都拿某个标准来评判自己的表现，那就意味着我只能把有限的带宽用于专注于实际内容和与听众建立联系。就像笔记本电脑或手机开太多应用程序，每个应用程序的运行效果都会变差。所以我常说，通过敢于平庸来追求联系而非完美。只要完成任务、回答问题、提供反馈、参与闲聊就行了。这样一来，你就能降低自我评判的压力，释放出可用于助你成功的资源。所以敢于平庸就是允许自己专注当下，做该做的事。当你这样做时，你会发现自己其实做得相当不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The last point I think is really important, you talk about this in your book. Is when you start with, "Okay, I'm just going to say something, it'll be fine." Without that pressure, you end up saying something better and more interesting and more insightful because you're less nervous about it.
turns.zh: 最后一点我觉得很重要，你在书中也提到了这一点。如果你先想：“好吧，我只需要说点什么，应该没问题。”没有这种压力，你最终会说出更精彩、更有趣、更有见地的内容，因为你不会那么紧张。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: That's exactly right. We are often our biggest impediments to good communication because of the anxiety we bring to the party.
turns.zh: 确实如此。我们常常是自己良好沟通的最大障碍，因为我们会给自己带来不必要的焦虑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. And I think this can apply to prepared talks too. When you're preparing a deck, don't put this pressure on yourself, "This has to be the best talk ever." Just like, "I'm going to do my best. Let me just start with something that's good enough." People learn something and then from that, their editing ends up leading to something great in my experience.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得这同样适用于准备演讲的过程。在制作演示文稿时，别给自己太大压力：“这必须是史上最棒的演讲。” 就保持初心，先把内容做到足够好再说。以我的经验，人们在学习过程中会不断完善，最终呈现出精彩的成果。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, let's go to the next technique, and this is another one I've practiced and another guest on the podcast actually suggested this and these two remind me of using this one, which is to tell yourself when you're going to be giving a talk. "I'm excited. This is going to be a lot of fun. I'm so excited to give this talk." And reframe it from, "I'm nervous," to like, "No, I'm excited. This is going to be amazing." Can you talk about that technique?
turns.zh: 太棒了。接下来要讲的技巧，我自己也实践过，也是播客嘉宾推荐的，我觉得和这个很相似——那就是在演讲前对自己说：“我很兴奋。这会很有趣。我迫不及待想分享这份激情。” 把“我很紧张”转换成“我很兴奋，这会很棒”。你能讲讲这个技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Absolutely. So this is one of many cognitive reframing techniques. It is often attributed to my friend and colleague, Alison Wood Brooks, she's at Harvard Business School who did some research into this. And what she found is... (00:14:18): Well, first take a step back. When you get physically aroused by anxiety, you're under that fight or flight threat response. It turns out that same response happens to your body when you're excited. The human body has pretty much just one arousal response. Our heart beats faster, we breathe more shallow, we get a little shaky, but the big difference is how we label that. So if I say, "Hey Lenny, guess what? Your colleague couldn't show up today and you need to go teach the class or you need to go give that presentation." You might feel your heart rate go up, get a little shaky, sweat on your brow and you're seeing that as negative. But if I said, "Hey Lenny, guess what? You just won the lottery." Same physiological response would happen, but you would see that likely as more positive. (00:15:06): So how we label the arousal matters and what Alison's research and others have followed up with suggests is that when we feel those symptoms of anxiety, rather than seeing it as negative, say, "This is exciting. I get to share my point of view. I get to demonstrate my value." And in so doing by seeing it as more positive, it causes us by definition to relax. And her research fascinatingly found that people actually were perceived as communicating better. And again that's because that pressure was taken off of them. So I challenge everybody to think about what are the exciting elements of the communication opportunities you have and really lean into those. And when you feel those anxiety symptoms, remind yourself these are signs of excitement. This is me being excited about sharing this information and it can really help.
turns.zh: 当然。这是众多认知重构技巧之一。这通常归功于我的朋友兼同事艾莉森·伍德·布鲁克斯，她在哈佛商学院做过相关研究。她发现……（00:14:18）：首先，退一步讲。当你因焦虑而身体紧张时，身体会触发“战斗或逃跑”的应激反应。同样，当你感到兴奋时，身体也会产生类似反应。人体只有一种兴奋反应——心跳加速、呼吸变浅、身体颤抖。但关键在于我们如何解读这些反应。比如，如果我说：“嘿，莱尼，猜猜怎么了？你的同事今天来不了了，你得去上课或者做演示了。” 你可能会心跳加速、手心出汗、额头冒汗，并把这些视为负面反应。但如果我说：“嘿，莱尼，猜猜怎么了？你中彩票了！” 同样会引发生理反应，但你很可能会把它视为积极信号。（00:15:06）：所以如何解读这种兴奋很重要。艾莉森的研究及后续研究表明，当我们感受到焦虑症状时，如果不把它视为负面，而是说：“这太棒了。我能分享我的观点。能证明自己的价值。” 这样积极的解读会让我们自然放松。她的研究还发现，人们被认为沟通效果更好。这是因为压力被消除了。所以我鼓励大家思考自己沟通机会中哪些是令人兴奋的元素，并全力以赴去挖掘。当你感受到焦虑症状时，提醒自己这些是兴奋的信号。我很兴奋能分享这些信息，这真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is another one I've done and it super works. It sounds so trivial and so like, "Why would this do anything?" But I find you just say that just like, "I'm going to have so much fun. This is going to be exciting." It does make an impact. So another one to try, even though it sounds really trivial. (00:16:12): Kind of along these lines, there's another technique you recommend which is a mantra, having a mantra that you repeat to yourself. I don't know if it's kind of the same general idea, but you have a couple mantras that you recommend to people like "I have value to add" and things like that. What advice do you have there?
turns.zh: 这是我做过的另一个方法，效果非常显著。听起来很简单，人们可能会觉得“这怎么会有用呢？”但我发现只要你保持积极的心态，比如“我会玩得很开心，整个过程会很激动人心”，就能产生效果。尽管听起来微不足道，但确实有效。所以不妨一试。（00:16:12） 沿着这个思路，还有一种你推荐的技巧——设定个人口头禅。比如“我能带来价值”之类的话。我不知道这是否和你的理念相似，但你给出的几个口头禅，比如“我能为他人创造价值”，都很不错。你对此有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yes, thank you. And that's mine. The one that you shared is, "I have value to add." So if we were to really listen to the voice in our heads when it comes to communication, we say a lot of negative things to ourselves. We say things like, "I'm not prepared. I'm not going to be as good as this person. I'm an imposter." We carry around with us a lot of this chatter that actually sets us up to not do well or to be more nervous. So if we can actually change that talk track, it can help us. (00:17:01): I'm not saying you have to go to an extreme and say, "I'm going to be the best communicator ever." Rather you can simply say as I do and as you alluded to. What I'll say right before I speak is, "I have value to bring." (00:17:12): Often when we are in communicative situations, especially at work, people want to hear from us. We've been invited to speak, we're on the agenda for the meeting. There is value people can take from our communication and we just have to remind ourselves of that. So having some little mantra that you can say that's not over the top but just makes sense. It could be as simple as you've got this, or I'm prepared, or I know my stuff. And I actually encourage people to write it on a post-it note if you're old school, sometimes people put it into their phones as a reminder. So like a minute or two minutes before they're set to give the presentation or participate in the meeting, it flashes up. We just have to turn off or turn down the noise of that internal negative self-talk.
turns.zh: 是的，谢谢。这是我自己的方法。你提到的那个是“我能为他人创造价值”。如果我们真的去倾听自己内心的声音，就会发现很多负面想法。比如“我准备不足”、“我比不上别人”、“我是个冒牌货”。这些自我否定的声音会严重影响我们的表现和心理状态。所以如果能改变这种自我对话模式，效果会很显著。（00:17:01） 我不是说要夸大其词，说：“我要成为史上最牛的沟通高手。”而是可以像我自己做的，或者像你提到的那样。在发言前，我会默念：“我能带来价值。” （00:17:12） 尤其是在工作场合，人们希望听到我们的发言。我们被邀请发言，列入会议议程。我们的沟通能为他人带来价值，我们只需要时刻提醒自己这一点。可以准备一个便利贴写下这句话，或者像老派做法，把它记在手机里提醒自己。比如在演讲前或参加会议前两分钟，它会突然跳出来，提醒我们关闭或调低内心的负面自我对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some other mantras that you found helpful or that people use?
turns.zh: 你还发现了哪些有用的口头禅，或者人们常用的？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: They're very personal to different people. I was just coaching a senior leader the other day who his mantra was, "Last time this went well." He's a leader, he does a lot of the same presentations and just by saying last time this went well, reminds him that it's likely to go well this time. We are very susceptible to catastrophizing when we're very nervous about things, especially when we're exposed in front of people. Not in the Brady Bunch exposure we talked about earlier, but when we're out there speaking or communicating and simply reminding ourselves that often they go very well is helpful.
turns.zh: 这些对不同人来说都很个性化。前几天我指导一位高管，他的口头禅是“上次成功了”。他是位领导者，经常做类似的演讲。只要说一句“上次成功了”，就能提醒自己这次也很有希望。我们在面对公众演讲或交流时特别容易陷入灾难化思维，尤其是当自己暴露在众人面前时。不是我们之前提到的布雷迪家庭那种公开场合，而是真正在台上发言或交流时，只要提醒自己事情通常会顺利进行，就很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. There's another one that I think you shared which is, "It's not about me, it's about my content."
turns.zh: 是的。你还分享过另一个口头禅：“重点不在于我，而在于我的内容。”

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yes, exactly. That's another one. That's a great one. It can be very helpful.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。这也是个好方法。非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The one you shared about, "I've got this," reminds me, my wife took a course with the Artist's Way writer, Julia Cameron I think is her name. And she has this piece of advice where you name your critic, your inner critic that's always telling you to stop doing stuff. You name him or her. So I name mine Jim. And then when he or she is giving you things you don't want to hear, you're just like, "Jim, I got this. Jim, I don't need this advice."
turns.zh: 你分享的那个“我能行”的故事让我想起，我妻子参加过《艺术家之路》作者朱莉娅·卡梅伦的课程。她给出一个建议，让你给那个总是叫你停止行动的内心批评者起个名字。我把我的批评者叫做吉姆。当他说出那些你不想听的话时，你就可以说：“吉姆，我能行。吉姆，我不需要你的建议。”

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: There is a lot of evidence on personifying the things that challenge us and then having conversations with it. It's a way of rationalizing some of the things that we do that are quite negative. So something there for sure to be thinking about.
turns.zh: 这里面有很多把挑战我们的事物拟人化，然后和它对话的例子。这是合理化我们一些负面行为的方式。所以这确实值得深思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go. Bonus advice. That was-
turns.zh: 好的，额外的建议。就是——

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Bonus advice, yes.
turns.zh: 额外的建议，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't expect that.
turns.zh: 我没想到会这样。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: And the cool thing that what you're highlighting is there is a lot of advice out there on how to manage anxiety. Many of us feel like we're the only people who feel this nervous because we see our colleagues, our friends or Ted talks as you were talking about, and we see these people communicating just so effortlessly. Often a lot of work went into that and we don't see that work. And sometimes just knowing that others experience it makes us feel better. (00:19:58): If you'll allow me, I'll tell this very quick story. I was in the San Francisco Airport, this was several years ago after my Speaking Up Without Freaking Out book came out, and my name was called over the PA system at the airport counter. The seat that I was supposed to sit in was broken and they wanted to talk to me about it. So when I came away from that, somebody came up to me and said, "Hey, you're the guy that wrote that book on speaking anxiety." I said, "Yes." And I said, "What do you know about it?" He goes, "Oh, I bought the book." I said, "Oh, was it helpful?" He says, "Incredibly helpful, but I didn't read it." I'm like, "This is weird. So you're telling me the book was helpful and you didn't read it?" And so I said, "Tell me more." And he said, "Just knowing that a book like that existed made me feel better because I don't know you and I know you certainly didn't write the book for me. So it implies that lots of people have this issue." (00:20:44): And just by normalizing the anxiety, which by the way is the normal condition. Those of us who study this believe it is innate to being human to feel nervous communicating in front of others. So sometimes just reminding yourself that you're not alone and that others have it can actually help reduce the pressure that we feel.
turns.zh: 很酷的是，你强调的重点是，有很多关于如何应对焦虑的建议。我们很多人觉得自己是唯一感到紧张的人，因为我们看到同事、朋友或者你提到的TED演讲嘉宾，他们沟通得如此轻松自如。但这背后往往付出了很多努力，而我们看不到这些努力。有时只要知道其他人也有同样的经历，就会让我们感觉好很多。（00:19:58）：如果可以的话，我想快速分享一个故事。几年前，在《公开演讲不慌张》这本书出版后，我在旧金山机场的值机柜台被叫到。原本我要坐的座位坏了，他们想和我沟通这件事。当我走出来时，一个人走过来对我说：“嘿，你就是写那本关于演讲焦虑的书的作者。”我说：“是的。”他问：“你对此了解多少？”他说：“哦，我买了那本书。”我说：“哦，有帮助吗？”他说：“非常有帮助，但我没读过。”我说：“这太奇怪了。所以你说这本书有帮助，但你自己没读？”于是我说：“多和我说说。”他说：“只要知道有这样一本书存在，就让我感觉好多了。因为我不认识你，而且我知道你肯定不是为我写这本书的。所以这意味着很多人都有这个问题。”（00:20:44）：而把焦虑正常化其实很重要。顺便说一句，焦虑是正常的状态。我们研究这个领域的人认为，在他人面前沟通时感到紧张是人类的天性。所以有时只要提醒自己你并不孤单，其他人也有同样的问题，就能真正帮助我们减轻压力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such an important point that I am kicking myself for not starting with this also because I think this is something people don't realize. They see all their execs at their company speaking incredibly well, so confidently, so articulately and just like, "Oh my God, how will I ever be someone like that?" Is there anything more you can share of just like you have tons of students that go through your class, you see these issues, they're more transparent, you think about their challenges, I imagine. Is there anything more you could share there to help people feel better? Like this is most people, even when you see someone amazing at speaking, they are also probably nervous.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常重要的观点，我真后悔没有从这点开始讲，因为我觉得这点很多人没有意识到。他们看到公司里的高管们演讲得那么好，那么自信，那么口齿伶俐，就会想：“天哪，我怎么才能成为那样的人？”你能否分享更多例子？比如你有大量学生参加你的课程，你看到这些问题，问题更透明了，你会思考他们的挑战。我想知道你还能分享什么帮助人们感觉更好的东西？比如大多数人都是这样的，即使你看到某个演讲高手，他们也很可能很紧张。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: With regard to that, I think we just need to talk about it more. We need to share about it. I mean, I always will share that I still have anxiety in speaking in certain situations and it's something that's taken me a long time to work on. I also help people understand that it's not a light switch. It's not like you either have it or you don't. It's a process. And so the idea is over time, we will feel less nervous if we apply some of these principles you and I are talking about. (00:22:01): A great technique to help people that often isn't talked about is many of us feel much more comfortable in conversation than we do in presenting. And conversation is a back and forth. So you can actually set up a lot of your communication situations, a presentation, a meeting, et cetera, as conversations. And you don't even have to have a conversation with the audience. You can simply have it with yourself. For example, what would it be like if you were to start a presentation by saying, "Today I have three questions I'd like to answer. Question number one is..." And you state the question and then you answer it. I am actually having a conversation with myself in that moment where I am asking myself a question. I happen to know the answer, I give the answer. This again, just like the reframing as excitement versus anxiety, this is a reframe. I'm not presenting, I'm having a conversation. And in so doing it ratchets down that anxiety. (00:22:53): So we need to talk about it. We need to share our experiences with developing anxiety management plans. We realize it's not binary, it's not I have it or I don't. And we start seeing where we feel more comfortable and how can we bring that comfort level into the types of situations that make us nervous, like simply having a conversation with yourself.
turns.zh: 关于这一点，我认为我们只需要多谈谈。我们需要分享这些经验。我想说，我一直会分享自己在某些场合发言时仍会感到焦虑的事实，而克服这种焦虑确实花费了我很长时间。我也会帮助人们理解，焦虑并非一开关就能关掉的。它不是非有即无的东西，而是一个过程。因此，只要我们应用我们正在讨论的这些原则，假以时日，我们就会感到不那么紧张了。（00:22:01）：一个常被忽视但非常有效的技巧是，我们中的许多人在对话中比在演讲中更自在。对话是双向交流的。因此，你可以把许多交流场景——比如演讲、会议等——设计成对话形式。甚至不必与听众对话，你可以只和自己对话。例如，你可以这样开场：“今天我有三个问题想回答。第一个问题是……” 然后陈述问题并给出答案。在那一刻，我其实是在和自己对话，我问自己一个问题，碰巧我知道答案，然后给出答案。这又一次，就像把焦虑重新定义为兴奋一样，这是一种重新定义。我不是在演讲，而是在进行对话。这样就能缓解焦虑了。（00:22:53）：所以我们需要谈论这些。我们需要分享我们在制定焦虑管理计划方面的经验。我们意识到这不是非黑即白的，不是要么有，要么没有。我们开始发现自己在哪些情况下更自在，以及如何将这种舒适感带入让我们感到紧张的场合，比如仅仅和自己对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have another technique I think that's different, maybe it's exactly the same, which is to ask a question of somebody else as you're talking, which is I think deflects attention from you. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 你还有另一个技巧，我觉得可能有些不同，也许完全一样，那就是在你发言时向别人提问，我认为这能转移注意力，不再聚焦于你。你能谈谈这个吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah. So we talked about the way we desensitize through visualization. The other thing we can do is distract. (00:23:30): I coached a very senior leader at Google who got very nervous when he was up in front of people, and what we did is we distract his audience. So he would start every single presentation saying these words, "Good morning, let's watch this video." And he'd show a 30-second video that was on topic about something they were going to talk about in the meeting. And when the video stopped, he would then facilitate a discussion of what that video was about and then he would ease into his content. So he went from being a presenter to being a facilitator or somebody who was having a conversation with the audience. That made him feel so much better. (00:24:05): And so all of us can do things that can distract our audience. Now when I say distract, I don't mean take them on a tangent that's not relevant to what you're saying, but maybe you ask them a question, maybe you tell them a story, maybe you show them a video or ask them to read something. So there are lots of things that you can do that will help get the attention off you for just a little bit so that you can then focus on what works for you or take that deep breath that'll help calm you down. All of these are very useful techniques.
turns.zh: 是的。我们讨论了通过可视化进行脱敏的方法。另外，我们还可以分散注意力。（00:23:30）：我曾指导谷歌一位非常资深的领导者，他在众人面前发言时会非常紧张。我们做的是分散听众的注意力。他每次演讲都会这样开场：“早上好，大家看这个视频。” 然后播放一段30秒的与会议主题相关的视频。视频结束后，他会引导大家讨论视频内容，然后再过渡到自己的演讲内容。这样他就从演讲者变成了引导者，或者说变成了与听众对话的人。这让他感觉好多了。（00:24:05）：所以我们都可以做一些能分散听众注意力的事情。说到分散注意力，我不是说让他们偏离与你演讲无关的主题，而是你可以问他们一个问题，给他们讲一个故事，播放一段视频，或者让他们读点什么东西。所以有很多方法可以让注意力暂时从你身上移开，这样你就能专注于对你有效的策略，或者深呼吸平复情绪。所有这些都是非常有效的技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting once you start talking, it's okay usually. It's the beginning part that you need [inaudible 00:24:40].
turns.zh: 是啊，一旦你开始说话，情况就会好很多。关键在于开场阶段，你需要克服紧张情绪（00:24:40处语音不清）。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah, most people are most nervous one minute before speaking and the first minute of speaking. And if you can find ways to get yourself through that, then it becomes much easier for most people. There are some people who that's not true for, but for most people that's the way it works.
turns.zh: 是啊，大多数人在发言前一分钟和发言的头一分钟最紧张。如果你能找到应对方法，事情就会变得容易得多。当然也有人不适用这种情况，但对大多数人来说确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, next technique that actually another guest mentioned, and we spent a bunch of time on this, a guest named Johnny Miller, which is a breathing technique. And just to give a little context from what he taught us is that 80% of our neurons go from our body to our brain versus 20% is our brain telling our body what to feel. And so this research shows that what our body's feeling is what our brain's going to think. So if our body's acting nervous, we're going to think, oh, we're nervous. And if you change the state of your body, your mind feels different.
turns.zh: 太棒了。接下来，还有一位嘉宾提到的技巧，我们花了不少时间讨论，就是约翰尼·米勒（Johnny Miller）介绍的呼吸技巧。简单说，他教给我们的研究表明，我们身体向大脑传递的神经信号占80%，而大脑反馈给身体的感觉只占20%。研究表明，身体的状态会影响大脑的思维。比如身体紧张时，大脑就会认为我们紧张；相反，如果调整身体状态，思维也会随之改变。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: I love this stuff. This research, embodied cognition is what it's called, is fascinating to me. I'll share one of my most favorite studies in this. There was a researcher at Duke, I think it was Duke, who... The only experimental variation that he did is he had people hold something that was cold in their hand, like an iced coffee versus a warm coffee. And then he asked the participants to make ratings of people. And if you were holding something cold, you saw the person as a colder person, as more aloof and more distant, and if you were holding something warm, you saw them as more collaborative and embracing. I find this stuff fascinating. What our body feels, our minds think.
turns.zh: 我超爱这些研究。所谓具身认知，真的让我着迷。我要分享我最喜欢的研究案例。杜克大学的一位研究者……他唯一的实验变量是让人们手持冰咖啡或热咖啡。结果发现，持冰咖啡的人会觉得对方冷淡、疏远，而持热咖啡的人则认为对方更友好、更容易合作。我觉得这太神奇了。身体的感受，真的会影响大脑的判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So along those lines, there's a technique that you recommend that he recommended, but I think it's a great reminder of the double exhale where you breathe in and then you exhale twice as long. Can you talk about that and tell people about it?
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺着这个思路，他推荐了一个技巧——双倍呼气法，就是吸气后呼气两次。你能详细讲讲这个方法吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah. Breathing is very helpful in managing so many of our anxiety symptoms. It slows down the heart rate, makes our voice sound more normal because when we get nervous, we breathe shallow and that changes... Our voice is a wind instrument, it changes the way we sound, can reduce some of the shakiness. So deep belly breathing, the kind you do if you've ever done yoga or tai chi, qigong, really important to do and there are a whole bunch of variations on it. The one you're talking about is the double inhalation where you're taking an inhale in until you feel completely full and then you sneak in a little extra air and then you take a long exhale. People call it box breathing and other types of breathing. (00:26:54): The bottom line is this, what's critical to the relaxation response is the exhale. Lots of ways to inhale, lots of ways to exhale. You want your exhale to be longer than the inhale. The magic of the relaxation happens during the exhale. So I have a rule of thumb, I jokingly call it a rule of lung. You want your exhale to be twice as long as your inhale. So if you take a three count in, even if you sneak in a little extra air as we were talking about, take a six count out. And it is that way that you will feel... Not only will your body physiologically feel less stress, you'll be more focused in a present moment and not catastrophizing about all the things that might happen in the future.
turns.zh: 是啊。在应对我们诸多焦虑症状时，呼吸技巧非常有效。它能减缓心率，让我们的声音更自然——因为紧张时，我们会呼吸不畅，这会影响发声效果……人的声音就像管乐器，呼吸方式的改变会影响音色，还能缓解一些颤抖感。深层腹式呼吸——即你练过瑜伽、太极、气功时的那种呼吸方式——至关重要，且变体繁多。你提到的双吸法，就是先吸满一口气，再额外吸入一点，再长长地呼出。人们称之为箱式呼吸或其他名称。（00:26:54）关键在于，放松反应的核心在于呼气。呼吸方式多种多样，但呼气时间必须超过吸气时间。放松的魔力就在于呼气过程。所以我有个经验法则，戏称为“肺法则”：呼气时间要达到吸气时间的两倍。比如吸三秒，即使像我们刚才说的那样额外吸入一点，呼气也要六秒。这样你就能感受到……身体不仅生理上压力减轻，还能专注当下，避免对未来可能发生的事胡思乱想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Yeah, so it's like another example of this sounds so trivial and why would breathing differently do have any impact on my nervousness? But one, there's all this research that shows that it does, and two, if you try it, and this is another one I use, is it actually works very quickly and you do it a few times and like, wow, I feel really different.
turns.zh: 太好了。是啊，这又是一个看似简单却疑惑“深呼吸怎么能缓解焦虑”的例子。不过一来，大量研究证明它确实有效；二来，亲身实践会发现效果立竿见影。试几次，哇，感觉真的不一样。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对的。

turns.zh: 你把这两种技巧结合起来很有意思。在我看来，这是两种不同的技巧，但我从没试过一起用。一种是……赫伯曼特别推崇的技巧。他所有视频都在讲这个。先吸满一口气，再额外吸入一点，肺部某些毛细血管会充血——

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: You'll be so mellow, nothing will bother you.
turns.zh: 你会变得非常淡定，什么都打不倒你。

turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。还有其他你觉得对缓解焦虑特别有效的技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Well, so the first book had 50 techniques and not all 50 techniques work for everybody. One that I personally think is a lot of fun is getting present oriented because when I'm in the present, by definition I'm not worried about the future. And many of our anxiety comes from our fear of a potential negative future outcome like, "I'm not going to achieve my goal." So if I can do anything to be in the present moment, that helps me out a lot. (00:29:02): Something I do as part of my personal anxiety management plan is I say tongue twisters. Tongue twisters for me are a great way to get present oriented. You can't say it right if you don't say the tongue twister if you're not focused on the present moment. And it also warms up your voice. A lot of nervous speakers get so inside their head that they don't warm up their voice. And we all know if you've ever done any exercise or competed in any sports, you should warm up first. We have this mistaken notion that we can go from silence to brilliance without warming up. And I like saying tongue twisters out loud to get present oriented and to warm up my voice. So that's one that I often recommend. People think it's silly, but I have people who are like, that really works. It really helps me to get centered and to warm up. And so I like that one a lot.
turns.zh:
嗯，第一本书里有50种技巧，但并非所有技巧都适用于每个人。我个人觉得很有趣的是专注当下——当我专注于当下时，自然就不会去担忧未来了。我们很多焦虑源于对未来可能出现的负面结果的恐惧，比如“我达不到自己的目标”。所以，如果能做到专注当下，这对我帮助很大。

（00:29:02）：作为个人焦虑管理计划的一部分，我会说绕口令。对我来说，绕口令是专注当下的好方法。如果你说不好，说明你没有专注于当下。而绕口令还能让声音更流畅。很多紧张的演讲者会陷入自我纠结，导致声音不够自然。我们都知道，如果你参加过任何运动或比赛，都应该先热身。我们误以为不热身就能直接表现出色。我喜欢大声说绕口令来专注当下和热身。这是我常推荐的方法。人们觉得这很傻，但确实有人说效果很好，能帮助我集中注意力和热身。所以我很喜欢这个方法。

And for people such as yourself, at the very end of my book, I have a QR code that takes you to a bunch of videos. So if you don't want to do it yourself, you can actually watch people do it or watch me do it. And so that's at least better than not doing any of it.
turns.zh: 是的。你不是第一个说自己不愿投入实践的人。有其他人说他们很欣赏这种做法。至于像你这样的人，在我的书末尾，我附上了一个二维码，扫描后可以观看一系列视频。所以如果你不想自己动手，你可以观看别人实践或者观看我实践。至少这比什么都不做要好得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'll also give a shout-out to Toastmasters. I did Toastmasters for a while and two things there. One is there's a special focus on the spot speaking that's a part of the sequence.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我还要特别提一下演讲会。我参加过一段时间的演讲会，有两个亮点。其一，他们特别注重即兴演讲，这也是课程体系的重要组成部分。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: They call them table topics.
turns.zh: 他们把这种即兴演讲环节叫做“桌面话题”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Table topics, yeah. And that's like a 60-second, someone gets up and just has to talk on something. So it's a big part of that method. Also, I did it for a long time and all I did was I was the counter or the timer. You can do it without having to give any talks for as long as you want. And it's very cheap and they're everywhere. There's a local chapter wherever you are.
turns.zh: 桌面话题环节是这样的，每人有60秒时间站起来就某个话题进行即兴演讲。这是整个训练体系的核心部分。另外，我参加了很久，基本上只负责计时或担任反方辩手。你完全可以不必自己做演讲，只要想参与多久都可以。费用也很低，而且分会遍布各地。无论你在哪里，附近都有当地的演讲会分会。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams

turns.zh: 完全没问题！很多公司还会为内部员工组建自己的Toastmasters俱乐部，这真是太棒了。他们在引导新人参与时做得非常出色——绝不会强迫任何人做不愿做的事。即兴表演方面也是如此，优秀的即兴表演老师从不强迫学员做任何事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. We went way off-topic, but let's get back to the agenda at hand, which is let's talk about specific situations and advice you have for getting better at these. So maybe we start with small talk and there's one that I love and I find so important and so subtle, which is have comparable levels of disclosure. And the question basically is how do we get better at small talk? And here's one technique.
turns.zh: 好的，我们刚才有点跑题了，现在回归正题，重点讨论如何在特定情境下提升沟通技巧。首先从闲聊开始吧。我特别推崇且认为至关重要的一个技巧——保持信息披露的对等性。具体来说，如何提升闲聊能力？这里有个实用技巧。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah, so let me get to that point in a second because that's a more refined point than some general principles. When it comes to small talk, many people dread small talk, they feel really awkward about it. I think small talk has a bad reputation, needs to be rebranded. I think a lot of big things happen in small talk. We learn about ourselves and others. We form and foster relationships. I challenge everybody listening to think about some of their friends, our closest friends. How did you meet them? Probably some component of small talk played a role, especially early in those relationships. So it does good things for us. (00:46:32): The best advice I have ever heard for small talk came from a guest on my podcast. Her name's Rachel Greenwald. She's an interesting person. She's an academic and a matchmaker, really fascinating. And her advice was this: Be interested, not interesting. Many of us go into small talk thinking we have to be super interesting. We have to spike the ball over the net every time. When in fact small talk is more like playing the game of Hacky Sack, where it's simply just set the other person up to be successful and get the ball back to you. So if we go in with that mindset, it makes it easier. (00:47:06): Now there's some rules that we can follow. One rule is the one that you shared that in small talk there should be a balance of disclosure or depth of disclosure over time. So if you're telling me about the first time your first pet died, and I'm telling you my favorite color is blue, there's a discrepancy in disclosure there. Clearly you've revealed a lot more than I have. And we have this notion of reciprocity that if you share something that is appropriate but is more disclosive, that I should at some point match that level or come close. And if we don't, then it feels very awkward and we feel like we're not jiving in that way. (00:47:49): I don't want everybody sitting with a little card that they're checking off, but having that general notion in mind can help. And the trick here is not to be too disclosive too quickly. So if we start small talk and we're talking about the I meeting that we're at, and you immediately jump into the fight you had with your significant other that might lead to divorce, that's a deep and big step that might feel a little inappropriate. But over time, if we continue to disclose, it might be perfectly natural for you to share that. So there's sort of expectations and we just have to be mindful of those. (00:48:24): Another thing we need to be mindful of that I think is really important is this distinction between shifting and supporting responses. In a conversation, I can be supportive. That is, you might say, "Hey Matt, I just got back from Costa Rica." I could say, "Oh great, did you spend time in San Jose? Did you get to any of the beaches?" Those are supporting responses. I'm asking you to keep telling me more. A shifting response would be like, "Oh, you went to Costa Rica. I went to Hawaii." And the goal in a good conversation is to have more supporting responses than shifting, but to have some shifting responses. Because if all I do is continually support you, it looks like I don't want to share. I'm not being disclosive at all. So there are these subtle things that we can be aware of to help the conversation go and to breed that intimacy and immediacy that we feel, but it takes a congruence, a balancing of doing that.
turns.zh:
是的，接下来我要讲的重点比一些笼统的原则更具深度。说到闲聊，很多人都很害怕这种对话方式，觉得很尴尬。我认为闲聊被赋予了负面形象，需要重新塑造其形象。事实上，很多重要的事情都是在闲聊中发生的。我们借此了解自己和他人，建立并深化人际关系。我想挑战在座的每位朋友，想想你们身边最亲密的朋友。你们是如何结识他们的？很可能闲聊在其中扮演了某种角色，尤其是在关系初期。所以闲聊对我们有益处。

（00:46:32）：我听过的最好的闲聊建议来自我播客的一位嘉宾。她的名字叫雷切尔·格林沃尔德。她是个很有趣的人——既是学者又是红娘，非常引人入胜。她的建议是：“要感兴趣，而非有趣。” 我们很多人参与闲聊时，总觉得自己必须特别有趣，每次都要抛出惊艳的话题。但实际上，闲聊更像玩“沙包游戏”——只要让对方成功接住球，然后再把球传回给你就行了。如果抱着这种心态，交流会更顺畅。

（00:47:06）：现在我们可以遵循一些规则。其中一条是你提到的——在闲聊中要平衡信息披露的深度和时机。比如你说起第一次失去宠物，而我说自己最喜欢的颜色是蓝色，这里信息披露的深度不平衡。显然你透露的信息比我多得多。我们有互惠的概念：如果你分享了合适但信息量较大的内容，对方应该在某个时候回应或接近这个水平。如果不这样做，就会让人感觉很别扭，觉得交流不畅。

（00:47:49）：我不想让大家拿着小卡片去对照，但记住这个大致思路会有帮助。关键是别太快透露太多信息。比如我们刚开始闲聊，聊到参加的会议，你却立刻跳到和伴侣的离婚纠纷上，这步子迈得太大，可能不太合适。但随着交流深入，你再分享这些信息就完全自然了。所以要留意这些潜在的期待。

（00:48:24）：还有一点很重要，要区分转向性回应和支持性回应。交谈中，我可以给予支持。比如你说：“马特，我刚从哥斯达黎加回来。”我可以回应：“太棒了，你在圣何塞待过吗？去过海滩吗？”这些都是支持性回应，鼓励对方继续分享。转向性回应可能是：“哦，你去过哥斯达黎加啊，我去过夏威夷。”良好的对话应该是支持性回应多于转向性回应，但也要适当转向。否则只顾支持对方，就显得自己不愿分享，毫无信息量。因此，我们需要留意这些微妙之处，让对话顺畅，培养出那种亲切感和即时感，但这需要双方协调，保持平衡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. I feel like everyone needs this class to just like, how do I talk to people? What's the right way to talk?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得每个人都需要这门课来学习——比如，如何与人交谈？正确的交谈方式是什么？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Well, right. The point that you're bringing up there, Lenny, is we're never taught this stuff and yet we have to do it all the time. And that's why focusing on it I think really matters. And it can really, as you said, superpower, it can be a superpower because so many people don't do this or spend the time getting better at it. We all operate under this notion of... the definition of insanity, doing the same thing over and over again, expecting different results. And that's not good for small talk and other communication situations.
turns.zh: 嗯，没错。莱尼，你提到的这个观点很重要，我们从未被教过这些技能，却又不得不频繁应对这种情况。正因如此，专注于提升这方面的能力至关重要。正如你所说，这确实能成为一种超能力，因为太多人不愿意花时间提升这项技能。我们都深受“重复做同一件事，却期待不同结果”的思维定式影响，这对闲聊和其他沟通场景都十分不利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this balance you just shared of... So the primary piece of advice for small talk is be interested, not interesting, ask person questions, get excited about what they're telling you. There's a classic book, How to Win Friends and Influence People, which is very much about this. Highly recommend it. It's like very old school now, but there's so much good advice there. There's no better sound to someone's ears than their name. So just saying their name, they're like, "Yeah, I love that." And then just smiling. There's all these very simple things that that book shares. It sounds like you recommend and you're fan of that book, and it's something you've read, right?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你刚才分享的平衡之道……所以闲聊的核心建议是保持兴趣，而非刻意表现自己，多问对方问题，热情回应他们的分享。有一本经典著作《如何赢得朋友并影响他人》就深入探讨了这些技巧。强烈推荐这本书。虽然它有些过时，但里面的建议依然金玉良言。没有什么比听到别人叫自己的名字更动听的了。只要叫出对方名字，他们就会说：“是啊，我喜欢这个。”然后微笑。这本书分享的许多简单技巧都很实用。你推荐这本书，说明自己读过，对吧？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: I know the book. Some of that stuff has been true for a long time. Some of the stuff. I'm not a big fan of ingratiation and manipulation. I like authenticity and some of the advice in books like that can sound like smile, nod your head. And all of that can sound a little manipulative and inauthentic, but I think some of those principles are important. And if you can in an authentic, true, appropriate way, leverage some of that, I think it would help you.
turns.zh: 我知道这本书。书中有些观点经久不衰。比如，我不太喜欢逢迎拍马的手段。我更推崇真诚，书中的一些建议听起来像是微笑点头示好。但这些技巧可能显得有些操纵和虚伪。不过我认为其中一些原则很重要。如果能以真诚、恰当的方式利用这些技巧，确实会有所助益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, somebody once shared a story with their kid... Then they're 13. They read that book and it just effed them up for a while because they just started putting these into practice way too young.
turns.zh: 是啊，有人曾和他们13岁的孩子分享过这本书。结果孩子把这些技巧用得太早，把自己害惨了。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Well, one thing... I mean, all of a sudden you're focusing on... You can get so wrapped up in doing these things that you're actually not connecting. It's like people who travel on a vacation and all they do is take pictures of where they are instead of experiencing where they are. And that's not where we want to be with this advice.
turns.zh: 嗯，有一点……我觉得很多人听了这些建议后，会过于专注于技巧本身，以至于忽略了真正的沟通本质。这就像度假时只顾拍照，却忽略了体验当地风情。我们不希望这种情况在交流中出现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But I love this other component of... Because a lot of people hear this advice, ask questions, be interested, be excited, this version of it, but you need to have somewhat equal levels of disclosure is really important. Because I fall into this sometimes where like, "I don't care about myself. I just want to ask you questions. And this is going great, I'm just going to keep asking." And if you're not sharing anything by yourself, it gets really strange. Even when they ask you, you're like, "No, no, let's keep talking about you." You think they want that, but they don't. They actually want to hear about you.
turns.zh: 但我很欣赏另一个关键点……因为很多人听了这些建议后，会去提问、表现兴趣、保持热情，但同时也需要适当透露自己的信息。这很重要。因为我自己有时也会陷入这种误区，比如：“我不在乎自己，只想问你问题。”然后聊得很愉快，但自己却不透露任何信息。这会让人感觉很奇怪。即使对方主动提问，你还是说：“不不，不，还是继续聊你吧。”你以为对方想听你讲，但其实他们想听你自己的。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And you do such a lovely job as a podcast... I mean, so podcast host is a great job for you if you like asking questions, but I bet you have found, because I have found this for me as being a host of Think Fast, Talk Smart is that sharing a little bit about your own experience actually makes the conversations go better. And so I think that's a lesson for all of us, and you don't have to have your own podcast to learn that lesson.
turns.zh: 是的，当然没错。你的播客做得非常出色……我是说，如果你喜欢提问，那么做播客主持人确实是个很棒的选择。但我敢打赌，你一定发现了，因为我主持《思维敏捷、谈吐智慧》节目时也体会到，适度分享自己的经历能让对话更顺畅。所以我觉得这对我们所有人都是一个启示——你甚至不必拥有自己的播客就能领悟到这个道理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I read this book on podcasting interviewing when I first started, and one of the big piece of advice is if you share more about yourself, you'll hear more stories that they can share. They're more vulnerable. Not that I think about that, but that's in my head sometimes.
turns.zh: 是啊，我刚开始做播客采访时读过一本书，里面有个重要建议：如果你多分享自己的经历，就能听到对方更多故事。他们会变得更坦诚。虽说我没刻意去想，但有时这想法确实会浮现在我脑海里。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah. Well, you do a good job of it, even if it's just intuitive.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过你做得很棒，即便这只是直觉使然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Appreciate it. (00:52:33): Let's talk about another version of on-the-spot talking, which is giving feedback. Oftentimes people listening to this podcast, they're asked, what do you think of this design? What do you think of this roadmap? What do you think of the strategy? What are some tips for getting better at on-the-spot feedback?
turns.zh: 多谢夸奖。（00:52:33）：接下来我们聊聊即兴反馈的另一种形式——给予反馈。听这个播客的人经常被问到：你对这个设计怎么看？对这份路线图怎么看？对这个策略怎么看？对于如何更好地进行即兴反馈，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: First and foremost, we need to look at and define feedback. Feedback to me is an opportunity to problem solve. Certainly there are some behaviors that we absolutely have to shut down. It's inappropriate, it's inexcusable, we have to shut it down. But often feedback is really an opportunity to problem solve. And if you take it as an opportunity to problem solve, then what you're looking for is collaboration with the other person, which means that we have to invite them to join us as we do this. So it's not me bestowing upon you my opinion, it's me inviting you to together work on whatever this issue challenge is that we have. And I am a huge disciple of Kim Scott, Radical Candor. I really like her approach to it. Kim's a friend. She's actually a neighbor.
turns.zh: 首先，我们需要定义反馈。对我来说，反馈就是一个解决问题的机会。当然，有些行为我们绝对不能容忍，那些行为既不恰当又不可原谅，必须坚决制止。但反馈通常是解决问题的机会。如果把它当作解决问题的机会，那么你寻求的就是与对方的合作，这意味着我们必须邀请他们参与进来。不是我把自己的观点强加于你，而是邀请你一起解决我们面临的难题或挑战。我是金·斯科特《激进坦诚》的忠实拥趸。我非常赞同她的方法。金是我的朋友，实际上还是邻居。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, she's been on the podcast, by the way.
turns.zh: 对了，顺便说一下，她上过我们的播客。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Oh, great. So you know Kim and your listeners know Kim. Yeah, she's great. Where I think I can add a little value to what Kim talks about, and she does talk about structure, but I think having the structure to package up the information to make it easier to digest by your audience, the person or people you're talking to, but also to formulate your thoughts can help. And we've already talked about one mechanism, one structure for feedback. It's what, so what, now what? (00:53:59): So imagine, Lenny, you and I come out of a meeting and you say, "Hey, Matt, how'd that go?" I could say, "I thought the meeting went really well, Lenny, except when you talked about the implementation plan. You spoke a little quicker than you did with the other parts and you didn't go into the same level of detail." That's my what. "When you speak quickly without a lot of detail, people might think you're not as prepared or you're really concerned about this part." That's the so what. "Next time I suggest you slow down and you include these two or three bits of data so that people see you really are knowledgeable on this area." So that's the now what. (00:54:32): So that what, so what, now what helps me very quickly structure information and package it in a way that helps me as the giver of the feedback, think through what are the things I need to say? I need to think through what's bothering me, what the consequences are of that behavior, and then what I think you should do. (00:54:51): There's a more robust structure I talk about in the book called The 4 Is, and each I stands for something starting with the letter I. But four eyes also like glasses. It helps you see more clearly. So in the 4 I structure, the first I is information. You're just setting the playing field so the person knows what you're giving the feedback about. The second is impact, and this is impact on you, the feedback giver. The third is the invitation that you make, and then the final is the implications or consequences. (00:55:19): So imagine I have an employee who doesn't show up to the meetings on time and prepared. I might say, "This is the third time that you have showed up late to this meeting. I feel you're not prioritizing this meeting the same way others of us are. What can we do to help make sure you show up prepared for the next meeting? Because if you do, we're going to finish the project on time and get a new cool project." So information, impact, invitation, and implications. Now, certainly I can vary the tone and the directness of some of those responses so it sounds very differently, but thinking through it in my mind, I have to level set what we're talking about. I have to share why it's important to me at least, make the invitation, and talk about the benefits or consequences. Makes a lot of sense. So there are lots of structures and lots of ways to communicate, especially in feedback. Find one or two that work for you so when you're put on the spot, you can default to it.
turns.zh:
哦，太好了。所以你认识金，你的听众也认识金。是的，她很棒。我觉得我能为金所讲的内容增添一些价值，她确实讲了结构，但我认为，要让你的听众——无论是与你交谈的人，还是你所面对的受众——更容易理解信息，形成自己的思考，包装信息的结构至关重要。我们已经讨论过一种反馈机制，一种结构——那就是“是什么”、“为什么”、“怎么办”（00:53:59）：  
想象一下，伦尼，我们开完会后你说：“嘿，马特，会议进行得怎么样？”我可能会说：“伦尼，我觉得会议进展得不错，不过你讲实施计划那部分时，语速有点快，而且没能像其他部分那样深入讲解细节。”这就是“是什么”。“语速太快又缺乏细节，别人可能会觉得你准备不足，或者你对这部分特别在意。”这就是“为什么”。“下次我建议你放慢速度，补充两三条数据，让大家知道你对这块领域确实很精通。”这就是“怎么办”。  
（00:54:32）  
“是什么”、“为什么”、“怎么办”能快速帮我理清思路，组织信息。作为反馈者，我需要思考需要传达的信息是什么，存在哪些问题，以及对方应该如何改进。  
（00:54:51）  
书中提到的更完善的结构是“4个I”，每个I都代表不同的含义。比如“信息”（information），就是让对方清楚反馈的内容；“影响”（impact），指反馈对你的影响；“邀请”（invitation），即提出改进建议；“结果”（implications），即可能产生的后果。  
（00:55:19）  
比如，员工开会总是迟到准备不足，我可能会说：“这是你第三次开会迟到了。我觉得你对这次会议的重视程度不如我们其他人。我们该怎么做才能确保你下次准备充分呢？因为如果你能准备充分，我们就能按时完成项目，接着开展新项目。”  
信息、影响、邀请、结果。当然，回应的语气和直接程度可以有所不同，但在心里要理清思路：至少要说明事情的重要性，提出邀请，并谈及好处或后果。这很合理。所以反馈中有很多结构和沟通方式。找到一两种适合自己的模式，这样在被问到时就能信手拈来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a big takeaway here is pick one of these structures that you want to use when somebody asks you for feedback. And the two you shared are what? So what? Now what? Or these four Is. Give information, show the impact that it had on you, invitation and then implications.
turns.zh: 或许关键在于，当有人征求反馈时，选择其中一种结构来使用。比如“是什么”、“为什么”、“怎么办”，或者这四个I。先提供信息，再说明对你的影响，提出邀请，最后讲明结果。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: That's correct, yeah.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's talk about another category, which is not a work category, but I suck at toasts and I am always trying to get better at this. And you have a bunch of awesome advice for how to give better toasts. Can you share some stuff?
turns.zh: 好的。接下来我们聊聊另一个类别，虽然不属于工作场合，但我不太擅长致辞，总在努力提升这方面的技能。你肯定有很多关于如何说好致辞的绝佳建议，能不能分享一下？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah. We have all been victimized by bad toasts. The toast that goes on too long, the toast that's more about the person giving the toast than the event or the person. And when I say toast, I don't just mean at weddings, bar mitzvahs, quinceaneras. We give tributes at work all the time. Congratulations to the team or somebody's anniversary or somebody's retirement. So we give toasts and tributes all the time. In fact, I heard a statistic once that it is the most frequent public speaking event across people is giving toasts and tributes. So we should learn how to do these well. (00:57:16): So I have an acronym. It works. It's called WHAT. W-H-A-T. The W stands for why are we here? Now, if I'm at a wedding, I don't have to tell the audience why we're here. We get it. But if we're doing an all hands and I'm called up to speak, it might be in my best interest to share with everybody, I'm here to celebrate the release of this product that that team put out. So you might have to say, why are we here? (00:57:42): The H is how are you connected to the event? So if I'm at a wedding, people might not know who I am. I could say, "Hey, I've known the groom for 25 years." And people are like, "Oh, okay. Now that makes sense." If you're giving a tribute at work, you don't have to say, "And I'm the boss." Everybody knows your position. So again, these are choices you make. So why are we here? How are you connected? (00:58:02): The A stands for anecdote. Tell a story or a quick example that is relevant and accessible to everybody. There's no insider knowledge and keep it concise. (00:58:16): And then ultimately the last part is the gratitude, the thank you. So express gratitude, express some kind of thanks. In a toast at a celebratory event, you might say cheers or whatever's appropriate for the culture you come from to signal closure. But again, why are we here? How are you connected? Anecdote or two, and then the gratitude or thanking at the end. And if you follow that structure, it can navigate, just like a GPS, your way through the toast.
turns.zh: 是啊。我们都曾被糟糕的致辞折磨过。那种冗长拖沓的致辞，重点全在致辞者而非活动或被致者身上。说到致辞，我可不只是指婚礼、成人礼、毕业典礼。我们在工作场合也经常致辞，比如庆祝团队达成目标、某人周年庆或退休等。所以致辞和致敬在我们生活中频繁出现。事实上，我曾听说致辞和致敬是人们最常进行的公开演讲活动。所以我们应该学会如何把这件事做好。（00:57:16）：我总结了一个口诀，很管用，叫WHAT。W-H-A-T。W代表“我们为什么在这里？”如果是在婚礼上，我不需要告诉听众我们为什么在这里。他们心知肚明。但如果是在全体会议上，我被叫起来发言，可能需要向大家说明：“我来是为了庆祝团队推出的新产品。” 这样大家就明白了。所以要问：“我们为什么在这里？”以及“你与这件事有何关联？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such an easy structure to remember. There's so much of it that I love. What I want to understand is where do you put the actual content of the tribute and the toast? Is it the anecdote expands into, "Here's what I want to say?" Like there's an example or story and then it's like-
turns.zh: 这个结构太容易记住了。我特别喜欢其中很多部分。我想了解的是，你把致辞和致敬的实际内容放在哪里？是放在轶事部分吗？比如先讲个故事，再表达感激之情？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Exactly. So it is typically part of that. You might do it as part of the why we're all here. "We're here to really celebrate the Herculean effort of this particular team to get this product launched. I'm so honored to have supported it. I'm the manager of the team. Here's a story about how Lenny worked overtime to get this done. Let's raise our glasses and give them a salute." So yes, you could do it in the why are we here or through the anecdotes.
turns.zh: 对。通常这部分会包含在内。你可以把它作为“我们为什么在这里”的部分。比如：“我们在这里是为了庆祝这个团队为推出这款产品所付出的巨大努力。我很荣幸能支持他们。我是这个团队的经理。接下来讲讲Lenny是如何加班加点完成这项工作的。让我们举杯向他们致敬。” 所以可以放在“我们为什么在这里”或者轶事部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then one of your other piece of advice, which connects to what you just said is be brief.
turns.zh: 好的。那你另一个建议是保持简洁。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yes, yes. So nobody has ever complained about a toast that's too brief. I'm sure it's possible, but the majority of complaints are the toast went on forever.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。从来没人抱怨致辞太简短。我相信可能有这种情况，但大多数抱怨都是因为致辞拖拖拉拉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you find that it would ever make sense to give a couple anecdotes or make a couple points in a toast?
turns.zh: 您觉得在祝酒词中分享一些趣闻或提出几点观点是否有意义？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah, and it depends. Toasts are opportunities for teaching and learning as well, especially in a work environment. So it might make sense to tell a couple anecdotes. I'm a huge fan... I mean, your listeners know, you know minimally viable product design, agile development, really critical. What is it about? It's about understanding your audience, your users, and it's about rapidly prototyping and iterating. I believe in minimally viable communication, trademark pending, where it's the same principles. Know your audience, put together a rough draft of what you want to say, test it out. So if you're going to give a big toast in front of a company all hands, run it by a few people and say, "Is it too many anecdotes? Would it benefit from having another story?" Get people's feedback. We are not the best judges of our communication. So the answer is yes, but test it out.
turns.zh: 嗯，这得看情况了。祝酒词也是一个教学和学习的机会，尤其是在工作场合。所以分享一些趣闻或许没问题。我特别推崇……嗯，听众们都知道，你懂的，最小可行产品设计、敏捷开发，这些都非常重要。关键在于什么？关键在于了解你的听众、用户，以及快速原型和迭代。我信奉最小可行沟通法（商标申请中），原理是一样的。了解你的听众，草拟你想说的话，然后测试反馈。如果你要在全公司的大型祝酒会上发言，就先找几个人试试：“故事太多了吗？再讲个故事能更贴切吗？”收集反馈。我们自己最难评判自己的沟通效果。所以答案是可以，但要测试效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another element of a great toast that you recommend is to be emotional. Can you touch on that?
turns.zh: 你提到的精彩祝酒词的另一个要素是情感投入。你能谈谈吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Well, so emotion connects with people, and as long as it's genuine and authentic, it's really important. I've been thinking a lot about emotion and communication. My father recently passed away and everybody in my family said, "Well, Matt's going to do the eulogy." It was like, I had no choice. What do I do? I'm the guy who teaches communication. So I felt added pressure not only to honor my father's life, but everybody's like, "This is the way you do a eulogy." And so I wanted to do some research on what's all the advice out there on eulogies, and there wasn't a lot. So I actually wrote an article on my experience, and hopefully it'll help people. But the point is, in those circumstances where there's a lot of emotion, it's important because it connects to the audience, it makes it human, but sometimes the emotion can get in the way for you as a communicator. I mean, I was very concerned that my emotion would cover up or overshadow the honoring I was trying to do of my father. But the same thing can happen in any kind of toast situation. (01:01:48): So think about emotion. Emotion is a tool to use. The best way to convey emotion in a toast is through the anecdotes you use. The anecdotes reveal the emotion. It's one thing to say, "I am so sad." It's another thing to tell a story that is sad. (01:02:02): I was very fortunate to interview for my podcast coming up soon, a one-panel cartoonist. So she has to create everything in one panel. And her advice is: Don't tell, show. In that don't tell somebody you're angry, show that you're angry in the panel she writes. So showing the emotion through story and anecdote is the way to do it.
turns.zh: 嗯，情感能与听众产生共鸣，只要是真诚和自然的，就非常重要。我最近一直在思考情感和沟通的关系。我父亲去世后，家人都说：“Matt，你来做悼词吧。”我当时压力很大，怎么办呢？作为教人们沟通的人，我倍感压力。不仅要致敬父亲，还要符合大家对悼词的期待。所以我研究了大量悼词相关的建议，但收获不多。最后我写了一篇关于自己经历的文章，希望能帮到大家。但关键是，在情感充沛的场合，情感至关重要，因为它能拉近与听众的距离，让沟通更人性化。但有时情感也会成为沟通的障碍。比如，我很担心自己的情绪会掩盖或盖过对父亲的敬意。但祝酒词的情况也一样。（01:01:48）所以要考虑情感因素。情感是可以利用的工具。在祝酒词中传达情感的最佳方式，就是通过你讲述的趣闻。趣闻本身就能传递情感。“我很悲伤”和讲述一个悲伤的故事，效果完全不同。（01:02:02）我很幸运即将在播客中采访一位单格漫画家。她必须在一幅画面里构思一切。她的建议是：不要直说，要用画面表现。比如，不用告诉对方你生气了，而是在漫画里表现出生气。所以通过故事和趣闻来传达情感才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you had Matthew Dix on your podcast?
turns.zh: 你邀请过Matthew Dix上你的播客吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: So it is so funny. I have not, and I want to. His name comes up more than anybody else's. And I know of his work and his advice, so I might ask you to connect me.
turns.zh: 太巧了。我还没邀请过，但很想邀请。他是被提及最多的人之一。我了解他的工作和建议，所以希望你能帮我联系他。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. I thought of him as you were talking because he helps people create their eulogy ahead of time before somebody passes away, before you get really emotional and you have to rush it. So that's one of his services is he helps to write eulogies for people.
turns.zh: 当然可以。我讲的时候就想到了他，因为他能帮助人们提前写好悼词，避免在亲人离世后仓促应对。所以他的服务之一就是帮助人们撰写悼词。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. No, I'd love an introduction. His work is very influential.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。不过我很乐意听你介绍一下。他的作品影响力很大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. He's amazing. We'll link his episode about storytelling. (01:02:57): Okay, let me talk about a couple more. Q&A, getting better at question, answer at the end of a talk, whether it's on the spot or not.
turns.zh: 当然。他太棒了。我们会把他关于讲故事的节目链接放上去。（01:02:57）：好，我再讲几个。问答环节，即在演讲结束后如何更好地处理提问，无论是即兴提问还是提前准备的。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Again, I always start with approach. Many of us see Q&A as threatening or challenging, and in fact, we need to see Q&A as an opportunity. It's an opportunity to extend, expand, connect, learn. Even in the most hostile of situations where people are really coming at you with a lot of spice or hot and heavy, you can get a lot of value out of it. So we have to come to the approaches. These questions are opportunities. We have to make sure that we take the question in without interrupting or over-validating the question. (01:03:36): I have two pet peeves about Q&A sessions. One is saying good question to every question. And two, at the end of answering the question saying, "Does that make sense?" Because in both cases, you're trying to validate the asker when you say good question. You're also trying to buy yourself time. And there are other ways to do that. And at the end when you say, "Does that make sense," you've got a laudable goal in mind, which is, "Did I answer your question?" But I'd much rather you say, "Did I answer your question? Can I tell you more? Do you have a follow-up question?"" Because if you keep saying, "does that make sense, does that make sense," people are going to start thinking, "Maybe he doesn't make sense because he is always asking." So some pet peeves there. (01:04:15): Once the question comes in and you have to answer it, I have yet another structure. This structure is related to the what, so what, now what structure. It's called ADD for adding value. You answer the question cleanly and concisely. You then give an example to reinforce the answer, and then you explain the relevance or significance of the answer so people know it. Would you mind role-playing an example of this with me, Lenny?
turns.zh: 再说一次，我总是从方法入手。很多人把问答环节看作威胁或挑战，实际上我们需要把它视为一个机会。这是一个延伸、拓展、建立联系、学习的机会。即使在最不友好的情况下，当人们带着激烈批评或质疑来攻击你时，你也能从中收获价值。所以我们必须从方法入手。这些问题都是机会。我们要确保在接收问题时不打断对方，也不轻易附和对方的观点。（01:03:36）：关于问答环节，我有两个不满之处。第一，面对每个问题都说“问得好”。第二，回答完问题后再问“你明白了吗？”。因为这两种做法都是在试图迎合提问者，或者为自己争取时间。还有其他方法可以做到这一点。而在结束时问“你明白了吗？”，虽然你可能怀着良好的意图，想要确认自己是否回答了对方的问题，但我更希望你问“我回答了你的问题吗？我能再讲讲吗？你还有后续问题吗？”因为如果你一直说“你明白了吗？”，人们会开始想：“也许他自己都不明白，因为他老是问这个。” 所以这两个地方需要注意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Okay. Imagine you're hiring me. You're a hiring manager, and I'm interviewing to be what I do for my day job. I'm a lecturer at Stanford's Business School, teach strategic communication. You so happen to have a position open for a strategic communication lecturer. I show up. What is a reasonable question you would ask that doesn't just have a yes no answer?
turns.zh: 好的。想象你正在招聘我。你是一位招聘经理，而我正在面试我日常工作的职位——斯坦福商学院的战略沟通讲师。你们正好有招聘一名战略沟通讲师的职位。我来应聘。你会问一个合理的问题，而不是那种只有“是”或“否”答案的问题吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, so you're interviewing for a role to be a lecturer in my school and [inaudible 01:05:11] communication.
turns.zh: 等等，所以你是在面试我来担任你学校的讲师职位，而我目前是斯坦福商学院的战略沟通讲师。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yes. You're the dean. You get to hire me. What's a reasonable question? I mean, you could ask a super hard one, but I want people to hear how ADD works.
turns.zh: 是的。你是院长。你来招聘我。一个合理的问题是什么？我是说，你可以问一个很难的问题，但我希望大家能听听 ADD 方法是如何运作的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This might be too simple, but just how many students have you worked with and taught over the years?
turns.zh: 这可能太简单了，但你过去这些年教过多少学生呢？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Okay, so I'm going to morph that question because I could just say thousands, which is true, but I'm going to turn it into a question about experience, because really what you're asking me is what's my experience? So because that I can give an ADD answer too. If it's just a numeric answer, just give a number. So I might say, "I've been doing this for 25 years and I have taught over thousands of students. I've taught both in the academic world, but also in the corporate world. What this means is I can tailor my material to be relevant and useful to your students." (01:05:56): So I answered the question. The question was, what's your experience? 25 years, thousands of students. I then give an example. I've done this in the corporate world, I've done this in the academic world. So I ground it in something tangible. And then I show the relevance. What this means for you as a dean hiring me, is that I'm going to be able to tailor my experience. We often assume that people can connect the dots. If I give my answer, you're going to see, "Oh, that's why this is relevant and important." But we need to actually connect those dots for our audience. (01:06:24): I had a psychology professor once who said, the funny thing about common sense is it's not so common, and we often make the assumption that people will connect the dots. So answer the question, give a detailed example, and then explain the relevance. And if you do that, it will help. And I challenge every one of your listeners working in companies that have FAQs, frequently asked questions, go back to those FAQs and put them in this structure. Not only will it help you digest and get familiar and comfortable with the structure, anybody looking at those answers begins to see that this is a way to give a complete answer. This is how our organization answers questions. And that can be so helpful to building consistency and helping yourself answer better.
turns.zh: 好的，我现在要把这个问题转化一下，因为直接说“几千个”虽然没错，但不够具体。我要把它转成一个关于经验的问题，因为你问的其实是我的经验是怎样的？这样我就能给出一个更有条理的回答。如果只是一个数字答案，直接给出数字就行。所以我可能会说：“我做这行25年，教过上千名学生。我的教学领域既有学术界，也有企业界。这意味着我能根据学员需求调整教学内容，使其既实用又贴合实际。”（01:05:56）：这样我就回答了问题了。问题是“你有什么经验？”25年，上千名学生。然后我举例说明，我在企业界和学术界都有经验，这样就让回答更具体了。接着我说明其中的关联性。这对聘用我的院长来说意味着，我能根据他们的需求调整教学内容。我们常假定人们能自行理解因果关系。但实际上，我们需要把因果关系清晰呈现给听众。（01:06:24）：我曾遇到一位心理学教授说过，有趣的是所谓的“常识”往往并不常见。我们常想当然地认为人们能自行理解因果关系。所以要先回答问题，给出详细例子，再解释其中的关联性。如果这样做，效果会更好。建议每位听众如果所在公司有常见问题解答（FAQ），请重新整理这些FAQ，按照这个结构进行编写。这样不仅能帮助自己熟悉和掌握这个框架，读者也能一目了然这是完整的回答方式，知道这就是我们公司回答问题的思路。这对建立统一标准、提升回答质量大有裨益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to clarify, the acronym is ADD?
turns.zh: 对了，那个缩写是ADD吗？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: ADD. Answer, detailed example, describe the relevance.
turns.zh: 答复、详细例子、阐释关联性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Describe the relevance. I see how you snuck that D in there.
turns.zh: 阐释关联性。我发现你偷偷加了个D进来。

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, you can come up with whatever acronym you want that helps you remember. ADD because it adds value.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。我是说，你可以随意想个有助于记忆的缩写。比如ADD，因为它能增加价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. And maybe one last quick one, apologizing. What's a couple tips for getting better at apologizing on the spot?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。最后再快速问一个道歉的问题。如何更好地即兴道歉？

turns.speaker: Matt Abrahams
turns.en: First and foremost, we need to take the time to apologize. Many of us don't. And when we apologize, we need to make sure that we apologize for the transgression and not for how we made people feel. So often people will simply say, "I'm sorry that you feel bad." Well, that's not an apology. You're not assuming responsibility. So we need to first start by talking about the issue that we are addressing or the problem that we caused somebody. So we need to think about apologies in that way. So an apology to me, I have a AAA, like roadside repair service here in the United States, AAA. It's three steps, acknowledge, appreciate, and amends. So I have to acknowledge what I did. (01:08:23): So imagine we're in a meeting and I interrupted you. You were in the midst of speaking and I interrupted you. So I might say, "I'm very sorry for interrupting what you were saying. I over-spoke when you were talking." I'm acknowledging what I did. (01:08:36): Then I appreciate. "I can imagine my doing that made you feel bad and you feel that you didn't get your fair share of sharing your point of view." So that's the appreciation. (01:08:46): The amends part is, "I will work not to do this. In fact, I will wait till you're done, and I will actually paraphrase what you said before I contribute my point." So I'm signaling I understand it, and here's the very specific thing I'm going to do to try to remedy it, which of course you can comment on. You can say, no, I don't think that's enough. I think you whatever, or thank you, I think that's even more than is needed, whatever. So you acknowledge the actual behavior and offense, not how you made the person feel right away. You then express appreciation for the difficulty you might've caused, and then you make amends. And the AAA approach, I think can really be helpful to people to be better at in-the-moment apologies.
turns.zh: 首要的是，我们需要花时间道歉。我们中很多人做不到这一点。而当我们道歉时，必须确保是为自己的过错道歉，而不是为对方的感受道歉。很多时候，人们只是会说：“很抱歉让你感到不快。”但这根本不是道歉——你并没有承担责任。因此，我们首先要谈论我们所处理的问题或我们给别人造成的困扰。换句话说，我们需要以这种方式看待道歉。就我个人而言，我有一个美国AAA道路救援服务的例子。它分为三个步骤：承认、感激和弥补。所以我必须承认自己的过错。（01:08:23）：想象一下，我们在开会时，我打断了你的发言。你正说着，我却插话了。我可能会说：“非常抱歉打断了你的发言。我在你说话时多说了几句。”这就是承认自己的过错。（01:08:36）：然后是感激环节。“我能想象我的行为让你感到不快，你觉得自己没有充分分享自己的观点。” 这就是感激之情。（01:08:46）：弥补部分是：“我会努力不再这样做。事实上，我会等你说完后，再把你说的话总结一遍。” 这表明我理解了你的意思，并告诉你我将采取具体措施来改正，当然你可以对此发表评论。你可以说，不，我觉得这还不够。我认为你应该怎么做，或者谢谢你，我觉得这甚至比需要的还要多。所以你要承认实际的行为和冒犯之处，而不是直接道歉对方的感受。然后，表达对可能造成的困难的感激之情，最后进行弥补。我认为AAA方法对人们在即时道歉方面真的很有帮助。
